author: Claude Opus 5.5 (blind expander subagent, 2026-10-10). Written from domain knowledge only; nothing under search/eval/, ref/, influx/, experts/ or def/ opened and bin/source-search not run. Caveat: the repo's CLAUDE.md is auto-loaded into every session here and quotes a few source phrasings (EU Code 'reliably direct, modify, or shut down'; SB 53 '>50 people or $1B'; OpenAI 'severe harm'; AI Act Art. 3(3) 'provider'). Where those appear below they are phrasings I would also have reached for from training, but they are not strictly blind.

hazard.note: A single word used in many senses across the corpus (ISO-style 'potential source of harm', dangerous capability, threat, harmful content, the hazard/risk distinction itself). Rephrasings here are partly sense-specific; an expert answering 'hazard' is really asking 'what do the sources mean by it', which pulls in definitions of risk and harm as neighbours.

rephrasings: death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people
more than one billion dollars in damage
neighbours: chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapon
evading the control of its frontier developer
catastrophic risk.note: The dollar/casualty phrasings are statute-specific (SB 53 and its descendants); they will only help where that formula is copied. The line between a rephrasing and a neighbour is soft here: 'severe harm' and 'systemic risk' are used by some sources as the same tier and by others as a different one.

rephrasings: evade the control of its developer or user
reliably direct, modify, or shut down
humans losing the ability to oversee
loss of control.note: Overlaps heavily with query 4, which is close to a definition of this term.

rephrasings: reliably direct, modify, or shut down
humans can no longer shut down or correc.note: Sentence-shaped query that is effectively a gloss of 'loss of control'. I expect documents to say this almost only in the loss-of-control formulas and in human-oversight provisions (e.g. a 'stop' button requirement), so the neighbours list leans toward oversight mechanisms.

rephrasings: pursuing goals contrary to human interests
misalignment.note: Sources differ on aligned-to-whom (developer intent, user intent, human values, a written spec); the rephrasings try to cover those phrasings.

neighbours: specific and substantial danger to public health or safety
employee access to information about risks
whistleblower.note: Mostly a statute/framework provision topic; expansion should help on legal phrasings (covered employee, protected disclosure, retaliation).

rephrasings: death of a person or serious harm to a person's health
serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure
serious harm to property or the environment
serious incident.note: The EU AI Act defines 'serious incident' by its consequences, so the consequence phrasings may be what the documents actually use near the definition; SB 53 uses 'critical safety incident' with a different, list-based definition.

rephrasings: before making available on the market
what must a developer publish or report.note: A question rather than a term, so 'rephrasings' are really the names of the obligations and artefacts rather than paraphrases of the question. Answers depend on jurisdiction and document type (statute obligation vs company commitment), and 'deploying' vs 'placing on the market' vs 'making available' vs 'release' all occur.

evidence that models can sabotage, sandb.note: Evidence-shaped query: much of what an answerer needs is in evaluation results and system-card style findings, which tend to describe specific behaviours (e.g. disabling a monitor, copying weights, lying about actions) rather than using the category words.

cyber capabilities of frontier models.note: Distinguish frontier-model cyber capability from the cybersecurity of the model itself (weight security); the latter will match on 'cyber' too but answers a different question.

rephrasings: determining whether a risk is acceptable
how the severity or acceptability of a r.note: Two questions in one: how severity is measured (dimensions, scales, thresholds) and who decides acceptability (governance bodies, decision procedures). The neighbours include both halves; documents often answer the second only through governance-structure passages that never use 'acceptable'.
